verdict.rationale: The decisive lexical fact is a tagging split on one orthographic form (the way the word is spelled). The Hebrew consonants alef-dalet-mem are catalogued as TWO lemmas (dictionary headwords): H0120 the common noun (man, humankind) parsed Ncmsa (common noun, masculine, singular, absolute) in 549 of 551 instances, and H0121 the proper name parsed Np (proper noun) in 8 of its 10 instances. The proper name carries individual biography: Genesis 5:3 and 5:5 give an anarthrous (without the article 'the') Adam who lived a stated number of years, begot Seth, and died, and 1 Chronicles 1:1 lists Adam, Seth, Enosh as bare names. The Greek lemma G0076 occurs in 7 verses (Luke 3:38, Romans 5:14, 1 Corinthians 15:22, 15:45, 1 Timothy 2:13, 2:14, Jude 1:14) and EVERY token is morphology-tagged proper noun (N-GSM-P meaning noun, genitive, singular, masculine, proper; N-DSM-P meaning noun, dative, singular, masculine, proper; N-NSM-P meaning noun, nominative, singular, masculine, proper), with no common-noun parse anywhere in the New Testament. The store records a direct lexical bridge from H0121 to G0076. Romans 5 builds on 'one man' (heis anthropos, written as 'of one' henos parsed A-GSM meaning adjective, genitive, singular, masculine, plus 'of man' anthropou parsed N-GSM meaning noun, genitive, singular, masculine) with the consequence reaching 'all men' (pantas anthropous), and 1 Corinthians 15:22 sets 'in Adam' (en to Adam) in strict 'just as . . . so also' (osper . . . outos) parallel with 'in Christ' (en to Christo), so the named individual is load-bearing for the argument.

scripture.force: The Hebrew reads 'the man' (ha-adam) with the definite article 'the', parsed as a common noun, and says he became a living being. This articular (with the article 'the') generic is exactly where the readings can diverge. But this same clause is the verse 1 Corinthians 15:45 cites and renders as the proper name 'the first man Adam' (ho protos anthropos Adam). The text itself moves from the articular 'the man' to the named individual at this hinge.

'And Adam lived' (wayechi adam) 130 years and begot a son in his likeness and called his name Seth. The lemma (dictionary headword) here is the proper name H0121 parsed Np (proper noun), anarthrous (without the article 'the'), governing wayyiqtol (Hebrew narrative past) biographical verbs of living, begetting, and naming. These are predicates of an individual with an age and a son, not of humankind in general.

'all the days of Adam that he lived' (kol-yemei adam asher chai) were 930 years, and he died. A bounded lifespan with a death notice is predicated of the named referent. A lifespan with a beginning and an end is a property of an individual person, not of the human race.

'Adam, Seth, Enosh' (adam shet enosh). The proper name H0121 stands first in a bare genealogical name-list beside Seth and Enosh, both individual persons. The grammatical form is identical for all three nodes, leaving no slot for treating the first node as a category while the rest are persons.

'of Enos, of Seth, of Adam, of God' (tou Enos tou Seth tou Adam tou theou). Adam is the terminal node of the genealogy of Jesus, parsed N-GSM-P (noun, genitive, singular, masculine, proper), in the identical 'of-the' (tou plus genitive, the 'from-X' grammatical form) construction used for every other named ancestor such as Abraham, David, and Joseph. The chain admits no grammatical genre-shift at Adam, so Adam is read as a real ancestor like the rest.

'through one man sin entered into the world' (di henos anthropou he hamartia eis ton kosmon eiselthen), and the consequence extends 'to all men' (eis pantas anthropous). The morphology is 'of one' (henos) parsed A-GSM (adjective, genitive, singular, masculine), plus 'of man' (anthropou) parsed N-GSM (noun, genitive, singular, masculine), a numerically singular one man. The one-to-all causal claim only carries if that one is a locatable individual whose single act has a real point of origin.

'death reigned from Adam until Moses' (ebasileusen ho thanatos apo Adam mechri Moseos). Adam, parsed N-GSM-P (noun, genitive, singular, masculine, proper), is named alongside Moses as the two fixed termini of a defined era over which death reigned. Pairing Adam with a concededly historical person across a datable interval treats both as points on the same timeline. 'a type of the one to come' (tupos tou mellontos) also makes Adam a pattern-bearing figure parallel to Christ.

'through the disobedience of the one man the many were constituted sinners' (dia tes parakoes tou henos anthropou hamartoloi katestathesan hoi polloi). 'of one' (henos) is parsed A-GSM (adjective, genitive, singular, masculine) and 'of man' (anthropou) N-GSM (noun, genitive, singular, masculine), 'the one man', and 'were constituted' (katestathesan) is aorist passive (a completed past action in passive voice), a past-completed constituting of the many as sinners tied to one past disobedience of one named man. The aorist (a completed past action) locates a single act at a point in time.

'through a man came death' (di anthropou thanatos), with 'of man' (anthropou) parsed N-GSM (noun, genitive, singular, masculine), through a man came death, paired with 'through a man came resurrection of the dead' (di anthropou anastasis nekron). The same one-man-causes structure as Romans 5, set in symmetrical referent terms with the historical risen Christ.

'for just as in Adam all die, so also in Christ all shall be made alive' (osper gar en to Adam pantes apothneskousin, outos kai en to Christo pantes zoopoiethesontai). Adam is parsed N-DSM-P (noun, dative, singular, masculine, proper) with the article 'the' (to), and the 'just as . . . so' (osper . . . outos) construction sets Adam and Christ in strict syntactic parallel as articular (with the article 'the') corporate heads. Withholding a real referent from Adam breaks the symmetry that supplies the resurrection guarantee, because the Christ side of the parallel is unambiguously historical.

'the first man Adam became a living soul' (egeneto ho protos anthropos Adam eis psychen zosan). 'man' (anthropos) is parsed N-NSM (noun, nominative, singular, masculine) and Adam N-NSM-P (noun, nominative, singular, masculine, proper). 'first man' (protos anthropos) is an ordinal claim, the first man, about the first member of a real series, and the clause quotes Genesis 2:7 in the Greek Old Testament (the Septuagint, abbreviated LXX). Paul pins the proper name to the formed individual of the Genesis narrative, the articular (with the article 'the') 'the man' (ha-adam) who became a living being.

'for Adam was formed first, then Eve' (Adam gar protos eplasthe, eita Eua). Adam is parsed N-NSM-P (noun, nominative, singular, masculine, proper), and 'was formed' (eplasthe) is aorist passive (completed past action in passive voice) of 'to form' (plasso), a completed formation act, sequenced 'first . . . then' (protos . . . eita), first then. The temporal-order claim is the warrant 'for' (gar) for a present instruction, which presupposes the formed referents existed in that order.

'and Adam was not deceived, but the woman, being thoroughly deceived, fell into transgression' (kai Adam ouk epatethe, he de gyne exapatetheisa en parabasei gegonen). 'was deceived' (epatethe) and 'having been thoroughly deceived' (exapatetheisa) are predicated of distinct named subjects, asserting that two persons had different experiences of deception. A contrastive claim about who was and was not deceived presupposes two individual referents.

'the seventh from Adam, Enoch' (hebdomos apo Adam Enoch). Adam is parsed N-GSM-P (noun, genitive, singular, masculine, proper) and serves as the ordinal counting-origin of a real generational sequence, with Enoch numbered seventh from him. Counting generations from a referent treats that referent as the first individual of a countable line.

'like Adam they transgressed the covenant' (ke-adam aberu berit). The token is tagged H0121 proper name Np (proper noun), reading Adam as a named individual who broke a covenant. The prefixed 'like' (ke) and the shared orthography (spelling) leave the form open also to 'like a man' or to the place Adam, so this verse is recorded as a complicating text rather than as decisive.

complicating_texts.resolution: In Genesis 1 to 3 the lemma (dictionary headword) is the common noun H0120, parsed Ncmsa (common noun, masculine, singular, absolute), glossed 'humankind' in Genesis 1:26 to 27 and 'the man' with the article 'the' elsewhere, which on its own reads generically. This is the real source of divergence. It is resolved in the text itself: the articular (with the article 'the') 'the man' (ha-adam) who in Genesis 2:7 became a living being is the very clause quoted in 1 Corinthians 15:45 as 'the first man Adam' (ho protos anthropos Adam), and from Genesis 4:25 and 5:1 onward the same form is tagged the proper name H0121 with biographical verbs. The narrative converts the generic 'the man' into the named individual at a fixed point.

Genesis 2:20 and Genesis 3:21 are the two H0121 tokens NOT tagged Np (proper noun) but Ncmsa (common noun, masculine, singular, absolute) even though glossed 'Adam', which shows the editors themselves located the generic-to-name transition precisely in Genesis 2 to 3 and split on it. This confirms a genuine lexical fuzziness at the hinge, but it is local to the transition and does not reach the unambiguous proper-name uses in Genesis 5, 1 Chronicles 1:1, and the seven Greek N-...-P (proper noun) tokens, so it does not unsettle the overall pattern.

'like Adam' (ke-adam) admits three lexical readings the consonants alone do not rank: 'like Adam' the individual, 'like a man' or 'like humankind' taking the common noun H0120 sense, or 'at the place Adam' given that an identically spelled place name exists at H0121A in Joshua 3:16. The store tags this token H0121 proper name, but the prefixed comparative 'like' (ke) and the polysemy (multiple meanings) keep it genuinely ambiguous, so it is left unresolved and not counted as load-bearing for the verdict.

'a type of the one to come' (tupos tou mellontos) could be read to make Adam purely symbolic and so non-historical. But 'type' (tupos) in the same author denotes a real person serving as a pattern, as in Philippians 3:17, 1 Thessalonians 1:7, 1 Timothy 4:12, and Titus 2:7, never a fictional symbol, and a type relation presupposes both terms exist. Adam being a 'type' (tupos) of Christ requires Adam to be as real as Christ within the comparison, so the type reading supports rather than undercuts historicity.

variants.note: All anchor verses lie outside the ingested ECM (Editio Critica Maior, the critical edition of New Testament textual variants) window of 3 John 1:1 to 1:15, so 'not_in_ecm_scope' is true and no CBGM (Coherence-Based Genealogical Method) apparatus applies. No load-bearing textual variant in Romans 5:12 to 21, 1 Corinthians 15:21 to 22, 1 Corinthians 15:45, Luke 3:38, 1 Timothy 2:13 to 14, or Jude 1:14 alters the proper-noun parse of Adam or the one-man-to-all structure. The 1 Corinthians 15:21 and 1 Timothy 2:14 readings carry editorial sigla (scholarly marks) in the bundle, but these touch word order and orthography (spelling), not the Adam referent.

competing_lens_verdicts.verdict: Adam is a real first individual whose acts have causal consequences in human history.
competing_lens_verdicts.rationale: The proper-noun tagging across both testaments carries it: H0121 parsed Np (proper noun) with biographical age, begetting, and death verbs in Genesis 5, the bare name-list in 1 Chronicles 1:1, the genealogical 'of-the' (tou plus genitive, the 'from-X' grammatical form) in Luke 3:38, and seven Greek tokens all parsed proper noun. The aorist passives (completed past action in passive voice) 'was formed' (eplasthe) and 'were constituted' (katestathesan) and the ordinal 'first man' (protos anthropos) and 'seventh from Adam' read the lemma (dictionary headword) as a singular person.

competing_lens_verdicts.verdict: adam is the generic the human or humankind, so the figure can be read as representative rather than as a unique individual.
competing_lens_verdicts.rationale: This reading rests on a real lexical datum: the dominant Old Testament lemma (dictionary headword) H0120 means 'man' or 'humankind', parsed Ncmsa (common noun, masculine, singular, absolute) in 549 of 551 cases, glossed 'humankind' in Genesis 1:26 to 27, and carries the article 'the' as 'the man' (ha-adam), through Genesis 2 to 3, and the editors leave two transition tokens common-noun tagged though glossed 'Adam'. On the strongest form of this lens the early Genesis material is about the human as such. Its limit is that it does not extend to the anarthrous (without the article 'the') proper name with a lifespan in Genesis 5, to the bare genealogical name-lists, or to the seven Greek proper-noun tokens, and it breaks the explicit Adam-to-Christ parallel whose other term is historical.

competing_lens_verdicts.verdict: Adam is a real individual and representative head whose one act is constitutive for the many, paralleled by Christ.
competing_lens_verdicts.rationale: Romans 5:19 'were constituted' (katestathesan), an aorist passive (completed past action in passive voice) constituting verb, with the 'of one . . . the many' (henos . . . hoi polloi) distribution, and the articular (with the article 'the') 'in Adam' (en to Adam) set against 'in Christ' (en to Christo), support a head-of-many relation. This lens treats historicity as the precondition for the representative function rather than as an alternative to it.

hermeneutics.notes: The lexical pattern decisively favors a historical-individual referent for Adam wherever the proper-name lemma (dictionary headword) H0121 or G0076 is used. The archetypal-symbolic lens is grounded in a genuine fact, the polysemy (multiple meanings) of the common noun H0120 in early Genesis, and is stated here in its strongest form, but it does not reach the proper-name uses or survive the Adam-Christ parallel. The federal-typological lens is compatible with, and presupposes, the historical referent.

stem_audit.notes: The stem asks whether Adam and Eve were real historical persons from whom all humanity descends. The lexical inquiry is the neutral grammatical question of whether the canonical authors use the form 'adam' as a common noun for humankind or as a proper-noun referent for a unique individual, and where the text shifts between the two. The store answers this directly through the H0120 versus H0121 lemma (dictionary headword) split, the Ncmsa (common noun, masculine, singular, absolute) versus Np (proper noun) morphology, the definite article 'the' on 'the man' (ha-adam), and the uniform proper-noun parse of G0076. Verdict unchanged from the prior file.

lay_summary: The whole question turns on one Hebrew word. The consonants for 'adam' are both a common noun meaning 'man' or 'humankind' and the proper name 'Adam', written identically. The lexical catalog splits them into two entries: H0120, the common noun, which occurs 551 times and is tagged a common noun in 549 of them, and H0121, the name, which occurs 10 times and is tagged a proper noun in 8 of them. In Genesis 1 to 3 the common noun is used, glossed 'humankind' in 1:26 to 27 and 'the man' with the article 'the' (ha-adam), through chapters 2 and 3. That articular (with the article 'the') generic is the real reason readers can diverge, and even the editors leave two transition tokens uncertain. But the text then converts 'the man' into a named person at a fixed point. From Genesis 4:25 and chapter 5 onward the same form is the proper name, anarthrous (without the article 'the'), and it takes biographical verbs: Adam lived a stated number of years, fathered Seth, and died. First Chronicles 1:1 lists Adam, Seth, Enosh as bare names side by side. In the Greek New Testament the name appears in seven verses, and every single token is grammatically tagged a proper noun, never a common noun. Luke 3:38 ends the family line of Jesus at Adam using the same form as every other ancestor. Romans 5 argues from 'one man', the words 'of one man' (henos anthropou), one man whose single act reaches all men. First Corinthians 15:22 sets 'in Adam' against 'in Christ' in an exact parallel, and 15:45 calls him 'the first man', quoting Genesis 2:7. First Timothy 2:13 says Adam was formed first, then Eve, and Jude 14 counts Enoch as seventh from Adam. The grammar of the name, the genealogies, the lifespan and the formation verbs all read Adam as a single person, while the open spot is only the generic common noun in early Genesis.
